statement: If a rational and a medial area be added together, four irrational straight lines arise, namely a binomial or a first bimedial or a major or a side of a rational plus a medial area.
heath_proof: Let AB be rational, and CD medial; I say that the “side” of the area AD is a binomial or a first bimedial or a major or a side of a rational plus a medial area. For AB is either greater or less than CD. First, let it be greater; let a rational straight line EF be set out, let there be applied to EF the rectangle EG equal to AB, producing EH as breadth, and let HI, equal to DC, be applied to EF, producing HK as breadth. Then, since AB is rational and is equal to EG, therefore EG is also rational. And it has been applied to EF, producing EH as breadth; therefore EH is rational and commensurable in length with EF. [X. 20] Again, since CD is medial and is equal to HI, therefore HI is also medial. And it is applied to the rational straight line EF, producing HK as breadth; therefore HK is rational and incommensurable in length with EF [X. 22] And, since CD is medial, while AB is rational, therefore AB is incommensurable with CD, so that EG is also incommensurable with HI. But, as EG is to HI, so is EH to HK; [VI. 1] therefore EH is also incommensurable in length with HK. [X. 11] And both are rational; therefore EH, HK are rational straight lines commensurable in square only; therefore EK is a binomial straight line, divided at H. [X. 36] And, since AB is greater than CD, while AB is equal to EG and CD to HI, therefore EG is also greater than HI; therefore EH is also greater than HK. The square, then, on EH is greater than the square on HK either by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with EH or by the square on a straight line incommensurable with it. First, let the square on it be greater by the square on a straight line commensurable with itself. Now the greater straight line HE is commensurable in length with the rational straight line EF set out; therefore EK is a first binomial. [X. Deff. II. 1] But EF is rational; and, if an area be contained by a rational straight line and the first binomial, the side of the square equal to the area is binomial. [X. 54] Therefore the “side” of EI is binomial; so that the “side” of AD is also binomial. Next, let the square on EH be greater than the square on HK by the square on a straight line incommensurable with EH. Now the greater straight line EH is commensurable in length with the rational straight line EF set out; therefore EK is a fourth binomial. [X. Deff. II. 4] But EF is rational; and, if an area be contained by a rational straight line and the fourth binomial, the “side” of the area is the irrational straight line called major. [X. 57] Therefore the “side” of the area EI is major; so that the “side” of the area AD is also major. Next, let AB be less than CD; therefore EG is also less than HI, so that EH is also less than HK. Now the square on HK is greater than the square on EH either by the square on a straight line commensurable with HK or by the square on a straight line incommensurable with it. First, let the square on it be greater by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with itself. Now the lesser straight line EH is commensurable in length with the rational straight line EF set out; therefore EK is a second binomial. [X. Deff. II. 2] But EF is rational, and, if an area be contained by a rational straight line and the second binomial, the side of the square equal to it is a first bimedial; [X. 55] therefore the “side” of the area EI is a first bimedial, so that the “side” of AD is also a first bimedial. Next, let the square on HK be greater than the square on HE by the square on a straight line incommensurable with HK. Now the lesser straight line EH is commensurable with the rational straight line EF set out; therefore EK is a fifth binomial. [X. Deff. II. 5] But EF is rational; and, if an area be contained by a rational straight line and the fifth binomial, the side of the square equal to the area is a side of a rational plus a medial area. [X. 58] Therefore the “side” of the area EI is a side of a rational plus a medial area, so that the “side” of the area AD is also a side of a rational plus a medial area.
ai_proof_text:
10.71
**Statement:** If a rational and a medial area be added together, four irrational straight lines arise, namely a binomial or a first bimedial or a major or a side of a rational plus a medial area.

**Step 1.** Let AB be a rational area and CD a medial area. Let the area (AB + CD) be the total area, and let a rational straight line EF be set out.

**Step 2.** Apply the area AB to the rational straight line EF, producing as breadth EG. Since AB is a rational area and EF is rational, EG is rational and commensurable in length with EF, by 10.20.

**Step 3.** Apply the area CD to the rational straight line EF, producing as breadth GH (placed adjacent to EG along EF, so that the total area AB + CD is applied to EF producing breadth EH = EG + GH). Since CD is a medial area, by definition D10.1.4 the square on a medial straight line is the medial area, and by 10.22, when the square on a medial straight line is applied to a rational straight line, the breadth is rational and incommensurable in length with the line to which it is applied. Thus GH is rational and incommensurable in length with EF.

**Step 4.** Since EG is commensurable in length with EF (Step 2) and GH is incommensurable in length with EF (Step 3), it follows by 10.13 that EG is incommensurable in length with GH.

**Step 5.** Since both EG and GH are rational (Steps 2 and 3), and they are incommensurable in length with one another (Step 4), EG and GH are rational straight lines commensurable in square only. Therefore, by 10.36, EH = EG + GH is a binomial straight line.

**Step 6.** Now the binomial EH, when considered relative to the rational line EF, falls into one of four possible orders depending on the commensurability conditions of its terms EG and GH with EF and the relation between the squares on EG and GH. We examine the cases.

**Step 7.** Case (i): EG is commensurable in length with EF and the square on EG is greater than the square on GH by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with EG. Since EG (the greater term) is commensurable in length with EF, EH is a first binomial by D10.2.1. Applying the total area (AB + CD) to the rational line EF produces the first binomial EH as breadth. By 10.54, the side of an area contained by a rational straight line and the first binomial is a binomial straight line.

**Step 8.** Case (ii): GH is commensurable in length with EF and the square on EG is greater than the square on GH by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with EG. Since the lesser term GH is commensurable in length with EF, EH is a second binomial by D10.2.2. By 10.55, the side of an area contained by a rational straight line and the second binomial is a first bimedial straight line.

**Step 9.** Case (iii): Neither EG nor GH is commensurable in length with EF, but EG is commensurable in length with EF fails, so we consider: EG is commensurable in length with EF and the square on EG is greater than the square on GH by the square on a straight line incommensurable in length with EG. Since the greater term EG is commensurable in length with EF, EH is a fourth binomial by D10.2.4. By 10.57, the side of an area contained by a rational straight line and the fourth binomial is a major straight line.

**Step 10.** Case (iv): GH is commensurable in length with EF and the square on EG is greater than the square on GH by the square on a straight line incommensurable in length with EG. Since the lesser term GH is commensurable in length with EF, EH is a fifth binomial by D10.2.5. By 10.58, the side of an area contained by a rational straight line and the fifth binomial is the side of a rational plus a medial area.

**Step 11.** We now show these are the only cases. From Steps 2 and 3, EG is commensurable in length with EF and GH is incommensurable in length with EF. Therefore the greater term EG is always commensurable in length with EF, and the lesser term GH is always incommensurable in length with EF. (Note: EG is the greater term because the rational area AB produces a breadth commensurable in length with EF, while the medial area CD produces a breadth incommensurable in length with EF; we may without loss of generality arrange that EG is not less than GH by choosing EF suitably, or we handle both orderings.) Given that the greater term is commensurable and the lesser is incommensurable with EF, the only relevant distinction is whether the square on the greater exceeds the square on the lesser by the square on a line commensurable or incommensurable in length with the greater.

**Step 12.** If the square on EG is greater than the square on GH by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with EG, then EH is a first binomial (D10.2.1), and the side is a binomial by 10.54.

**Step 13.** If the square on EG is greater than the square on GH by the square on a straight line incommensurable in length with EG, then EH is a fourth binomial (D10.2.4), and the side is a major straight line by 10.57.

**Step 14.** Similarly, if EG happens to be the lesser term (i.e., EG < GH), then EG is commensurable with EF and GH is incommensurable with EF, so the lesser term is commensurable with EF. If the square on GH exceeds the square on EG by the square on a line commensurable in length with GH, then EH is a second binomial (D10.2.2) and the side is a first bimedial by 10.55. If that excess square is on a line incommensurable with GH, then EH is a fifth binomial (D10.2.5) and the side is the side of a rational plus a medial area by 10.58.

**Step 15.** Therefore, depending on these conditions, the side of the sum of a rational and a medial area is one of exactly four irrational straight lines: a binomial, a first bimedial, a major, or a side of a rational plus a medial area. Q.E.D.
